The backend is split into three tiers: an API gateway that handles auth, a service layer that runs business logic, and a PostgreSQL database that stores all persistent state.
Our web app has a React frontend talking to a FastAPI backend, with Redis sitting in front of the database as a cache.
The platform consists of a message broker, a pool of worker processes that consume from it, and a result store that clients poll for completion.
The microservices talk to each other through a central service mesh, and each service owns its own database.
The system is organized as a load balancer in front of stateless app servers, with a shared Postgres primary and two read replicas behind them.
The mobile app sends requests to a GraphQL gateway, which fans out to three backing REST services.
The chat service is made up of a websocket layer, a message-fanout worker, and a Cassandra cluster for message history.

Writes flow into the primary Postgres instance, replicate asynchronously to two standbys, and reads are routed through PgBouncer which distributes them across the replicas based on a hashed session id.
The auth service sits behind the API gateway, issues short-lived JWTs, and every downstream service verifies tokens locally using a shared JWKS endpoint refreshed every hour.
The search stack has an ingestion service that writes documents to Kafka, an indexer that consumes the topic and pushes to OpenSearch, and a query API that reads directly from the OpenSearch cluster.
Our billing system uses an event-sourced ledger in Postgres, a projection worker that materializes account balances into Redis, and a reconciliation job that runs nightly against Stripe.
The recommendation engine is split into a feature store backed by Feast, a batch trainer that runs on Airflow, and an online scorer deployed as a gRPC service behind Envoy.
The API fronts three internal services: orders backed by MySQL, inventory backed by DynamoDB, and pricing which is a stateless computation layer that caches lookups in Memcached.
The notification pipeline consists of a publisher SDK in each service, a Kafka topic per channel, and per-channel dispatcher workers that write to SendGrid, Twilio, and APNs respectively.
The rendering server receives jobs over AMQP, dispatches them to a pool of GPU workers, persists intermediate frames to S3, and notifies clients via a websocket gateway when rendering completes.

The admin dashboard is a Next.js app that reads aggregates from a materialized view refreshed every five minutes, while live operational data comes through a websocket subscription to the events service.
The session store uses Redis in cluster mode with six shards, fronted by a connection pooler, and each app instance maintains a local LRU cache of the last hundred sessions to absorb hot-key load.

The write path accepts idempotent commands at the gateway, appends them to a per-tenant event log in Kafka, projects them into tenant-specific Postgres schemas, and exposes snapshots over a read-only gRPC service that clients reach through a regional CDN edge.

The feature platform layers a streaming feature computer on top of Flink, a point-in-time correct training store in S3 partitioned by entity and event time, and an online store in ScyllaDB that the serving layer reads with a strict fifteen-millisecond SLA.

Each tenant's data is sharded across a cluster of Vitess keyspaces, routed by a custom query planner that inspects the tenant id in every incoming request, with cross-shard queries served by a lambda architecture that joins Hive batch results against Kafka-sourced streaming deltas.

The API boundary is a Kong gateway enforcing OAuth scopes, behind it sits a BFF layer per client type, which calls into domain services that communicate through a combination of synchronous gRPC for queries and an AsyncAPI-described event bus for state changes.

The storage layer is split into a hot tier in NVMe-backed Postgres, a warm tier in columnar ClickHouse reached through a tiering service that migrates partitions older than thirty days, and a cold tier in S3 Glacier queried through Athena for audit requests.

The multi-region deployment runs an active-active Cassandra ring for user data, region-pinned Postgres for orders with conflict-free merge semantics enforced by a CRDT-backed reconciliation worker, and a single global Spanner instance for billing that all regions read and write with strong consistency.

Client requests hit a global Anycast edge, are routed by geo-affinity to a regional API tier that terminates TLS, authenticates against a replicated Keycloak cluster, and dispatches work to regional services whose outputs are streamed back through server-sent events for long-running operations.

The core platform exposes a CQRS boundary: commands land on NATS JetStream and are serialized per aggregate by a partitioning layer, while queries hit a Dgraph cluster populated by a separate projector service that subscribes to the same stream and maintains eventually consistent read models.

The object service is a three-zone Ceph cluster with erasure-coded pools for cold buckets and replicated pools for hot buckets, fronted by a MinIO gateway that translates S3 API calls, with tenant isolation enforced by a sidecar that rewrites bucket names using a tenant-scoped prefix.

The search topology uses OpenSearch for keyword lookup, Qdrant for vector similarity, and a fusion layer that reciprocally ranks results from both, with a feature-flagged reranker stage backed by a cross-encoder hosted on Triton Inference Server.

The identity plane is split into an authenticator that issues first-party tokens, an authorizer that evaluates Cedar policies against a replicated decision cache, and a credential broker that mints short-lived cloud credentials on demand through STS AssumeRoleWithWebIdentity.

The runtime is a hierarchy of controllers: a top-level orchestrator watches declared workloads in etcd, per-workload reconcilers translate them into pods, and node-level agents enforce the final state while reporting deltas back through a bidirectional gRPC stream.

Our realtime collaboration stack layers a CRDT engine per document, a presence service backed by Redis pub/sub, a persistence worker that snapshots every thirty seconds into Postgres, and an operational transform bridge that lets legacy clients without CRDT support continue editing.
The data pipeline ingests events through Kafka, processes them in a Spark Structured Streaming job, and writes the results into a Delta Lake table.
Raw logs land in S3, a scheduled Glue job normalizes them, and the cleaned data is loaded into Snowflake for analysts to query.
The ETL flow goes from the source database through Fivetran into BigQuery, then dbt models transform the raw tables into marts.
Sensors publish readings to MQTT, a Telegraf agent forwards them into InfluxDB, and Grafana dashboards read directly from the time-series store.
The ingestion tier writes raw events to Kinesis, Lambda consumers enrich them, and the enriched stream is dropped into Redshift for reporting.

The CDC pipeline captures Postgres writes via Debezium, publishes them to Kafka, applies schema evolution through the Schema Registry, and lands the events in Iceberg tables partitioned by ingestion date.

Clickstream events are batched at the edge, uploaded to S3 every minute, consumed by an Airflow DAG that runs hourly, validated with Great Expectations, and loaded into Snowflake where dbt materializes the reporting layer.
The analytics pipeline has two lanes: a realtime lane using Flink for sub-second aggregates over Kafka, and a batch lane using Spark on EMR that reprocesses the previous day's data for correctness.

The feature extraction flow reads raw events from S3, runs a sequence of Beam pipelines on Dataflow for cleansing and joining, writes parquet outputs back to S3, and registers the result as a versioned table in the Hive metastore.

Medical images arrive through an SFTP drop, a Python worker anonymizes them and writes to an encrypted S3 bucket, a downstream Step Functions workflow invokes SageMaker for inference, and the annotated outputs are pushed to a DICOM server.

Our fraud detection pipeline ingests transactions through Kafka, runs a Flink job that joins them against a rolling user-profile table in RocksDB, scores each one with an ONNX model, and writes flagged cases to a Postgres queue consumed by the manual review UI.

The marketing data flow pulls from Salesforce, HubSpot, and Stripe through Airbyte, lands the raw tables in BigQuery, transforms them with dbt into a common customer model, and exposes the result through Reverse ETL via Hightouch back into the source tools.

Legal documents enter the pipeline via an upload API, are OCR-processed by a Tesseract worker, passed through an entity extractor into a Neo4j graph, and indexed for full-text search in Elasticsearch for downstream retrieval.

The IoT telemetry pipeline runs device messages through AWS IoT Core, into Kinesis, down to a pair of Lambdas that fork the stream into Timestream for dashboards and S3 for long-term retention, with a daily Athena rollup producing device-health summaries.

The analytics warehouse has a staging schema populated by hourly Airflow jobs, an intermediate schema with dbt-maintained models, and a mart schema that serves both the BI tool and a reverse-ETL process feeding the customer-facing API.

The event backbone is a multi-tenant Pulsar cluster with per-tenant namespaces, bronze/silver/gold medallion layers stored as Iceberg tables in MinIO, a Flink-based stream processor that maintains silver projections, and a Trino query layer that the BI tier reads with row-level access controls enforced through Apache Ranger.

Our genomics pipeline ingests FASTQ files into a sequencing bucket, a Nextflow workflow triggered by S3 events runs alignment on Batch, calls variants with GATK on a Spark cluster, annotates them through VEP, and lands the final VCFs in a partitioned Parquet lake indexed by sample and chromosome.

The revenue data pipeline has a bronze layer capturing raw Stripe webhooks via Kafka Connect, a silver layer where a Spark job joins them against invoice snapshots, a gold layer of SCD-2 dimension tables maintained by a Delta Live Tables job, and a semantic layer in Cube that every reporting tool queries.

Video uploads are chunked at the edge, transcoded by a pool of FFmpeg workers orchestrated through a Celery queue, manifests are written to a CDN origin bucket, and a machine-learning enrichment branch extracts captions and thumbnails and feeds them back into the search index through a downstream indexing stream.

The ad-bidding pipeline runs a Kappa architecture on a single Kafka log: impression events feed an online aggregator that publishes minute-level counters to Redis, a replay consumer rebuilds daily rollups in ClickHouse from the same log, and all downstream dashboards read from ClickHouse with the Redis tier providing sub-second freshness.

Trading data flows through three concentric loops: an ultra-low-latency loop on FPGAs reacting to the multicast market feed, a mid-latency loop on kdb+ computing signals over the last five minutes, and a batch loop on Spark reprocessing the full day's ticks nightly to produce reference analytics.

The observability pipeline ingests traces into Tempo, logs into Loki, and metrics into Mimir, with an OpenTelemetry collector tier performing tail sampling for traces, log parsing with LogQL transformers, and metric relabeling before sharding each signal across per-tenant storage backends.

Our search indexing pipeline maintains a primary index refreshed by a streaming Kafka consumer, a shadow index rebuilt nightly from the source of truth to correct drift, and a delta merger that nightly diffs the two and emits correction events consumed by the primary indexer.

The ML feature pipeline splits online and offline paths from a single feature definition: the online path materializes into Redis through a Flink job keyed by entity, the offline path writes Parquet files into a training bucket through a Beam job, and a consistency checker periodically samples both paths to ensure point-in-time parity.

The compliance pipeline ingests every mutation event into an append-only audit topic, streams them into an immutable QLDB ledger, forks a second stream into a searchable Postgres mirror for investigators, and nightly exports encrypted snapshots to a WORM-compliant S3 Object Lock bucket.
The Kubernetes cluster has three control-plane nodes across three availability zones and six worker nodes, with ingress handled by an NGINX controller behind a cloud load balancer.
Our CI pipeline runs lint on pull-request open, tests on every push, and a deploy stage that only triggers when the main branch is tagged.
The network is carved into a public VPC for the load balancers, a private VPC for app servers, and a database VPC that only the app VPC can reach through a peering connection.
We run a three-node Proxmox cluster with shared Ceph storage, and each VM is backed up nightly to an offsite NAS.

The production environment runs on EKS across three availability zones, stateful services use EBS-backed PersistentVolumeClaims, and cross-AZ traffic is minimized by topology-aware routing on the service mesh.

The CI/CD flow is staged: GitHub Actions runs unit tests and builds container images tagged with the commit SHA, ArgoCD watches a config repo and progressively rolls out to dev, staging, and production clusters in that order.

Our homelab network has a Proxmox host running pfSense as the router, a VLAN for trusted devices, a VLAN for IoT with no internet egress to other VLANs, and a guest VLAN with a captive portal managed through UniFi.

The build system caches dependencies in a tier of three layers: a per-job ephemeral cache on the runner, a shared warm cache in S3 for the last twenty-four hours, and a cold archival cache in Glacier for historical artifact reproducibility.

The development platform exposes three environments sharing the same topology: each one is a dedicated Kubernetes namespace with its own Postgres via Crunchy Operator, an isolated Kafka cluster, and network policies preventing any cross-environment traffic.

The container registry sits behind Harbor with vulnerability scanning, promotion between project repositories requires a signed attestation, and only images with a passing Sigstore signature can be pulled into the production cluster by the admission controller.

Our multi-cluster federation runs a primary EKS cluster per region plus a single control plane in Argo that reconciles workloads across all of them, with Cilium Cluster Mesh providing flat pod-to-pod networking and a global Envoy tier handling cross-region traffic shaping through EWMA-weighted load balancing.

The CI platform uses a hierarchy of workflows: repository-level GitHub Actions build artifacts, an organization-level reusable workflow signs and uploads them to an internal OCI registry, and a Jenkins orchestrator triggered by webhook consumes those signed artifacts to deploy through Spinnaker to the final environments with canary analysis on each stage.

The network topology follows a hub-and-spoke design with a transit gateway connecting production, staging, and shared-services VPCs, private endpoints into each AWS service, AWS Network Firewall on the egress path performing domain-based filtering, and a separate inspection VPC that mirrors all north-south traffic to an IDS through VPC traffic mirroring.

The disaster-recovery architecture runs warm standby in a second region with Aurora Global Database for the transactional store, S3 cross-region replication for object data, and a Route 53 health-checked failover record pointing at whichever region's ALB is currently serving, with RPO under thirty seconds and RTO under five minutes.

The deployment pipeline for regulated workloads has four gated stages: a sandbox that any engineer can push to, a staging environment that requires a passing contract-test suite, a pre-prod environment that requires dual sign-off recorded in Jira and a successful automated compliance scan, and a production rollout that only a release manager can trigger and that applies progressive traffic shifting over four hours.

Our zero-trust network is structured around a SPIFFE identity plane issuing workload certificates, an Istio mesh enforcing mTLS and authorization policies between services, and a Tailscale overlay for operator access that tunnels every admin action through a bastion recording session transcripts to an immutable audit bucket.

The edge infrastructure places a Cloudflare Workers tier in front of the origin, behind it a pair of regional Anycast load balancers, each fronting a full-stack deployment with its own Postgres follower promoted to writer during regional failover, with DNS steering driven by real-user measurements collected through a beacon script.

The internal platform runs a developer portal powered by Backstage, a self-service provisioning layer built on Terraform modules exposed through a Crossplane API, and a compliance guardrail system implemented as OPA policies that run at plan time on every change through an Atlantis workflow.

The build-farm architecture uses a pool of autoscaling spot instances for general CI, a small reserved pool for cryptographically signed release builds with dedicated HSMs, and a hermetic Bazel remote-execution cluster that both pools delegate their compilation steps into for cache sharing across the organization.

Our observability backplane tees every signal across three independent stacks: a primary Grafana Cloud tenant for day-to-day use, a self-hosted Mimir + Loki cluster in an isolated VPC for audit-grade retention, and a third-party SIEM receiving only security-relevant events through a filtering Vector pipeline that enforces a strict allowlist of fields.
Our on-call rotation has two tiers: a primary who takes the first page and a secondary who gets paged if the primary doesn't acknowledge in ten minutes.
Code reviews require one approval from a teammate and a passing CI run before merge, and any database migration needs a second approval from a senior engineer.
The team runs two-week sprints with a Monday planning, a mid-sprint check-in on the second Thursday, and a retro at the end.
Our hiring loop has a recruiter screen, a technical phone screen, an onsite with four interviews, and a final hiring-committee review.

Incidents move through three severity levels: a Sev-3 is handled entirely by the on-call engineer with a Slack thread, a Sev-2 triggers a dedicated incident channel and a commander, and a Sev-1 adds a communications lead who posts hourly updates to the status page.

The code-review process is structured as a self-review before opening a pull request, an automated review by the linting bot and the security scanner, peer review from at least one engineer in the owning team, and a final maintainer approval for files flagged as sensitive in CODEOWNERS.

Our on-call rotation spans two time zones: a primary in Europe covers business hours, a primary in the Americas covers the remaining hours, and a week-long secondary handles escalations across both regions while the respective primary is offline.

The sprint cadence is a two-week rhythm with planning split into a goals meeting on Monday morning, scoping and estimation on Tuesday afternoon, daily async standups in Slack, and a demo plus retro on the second Friday.

Our security review workflow has three stages: self-assessment against a questionnaire in the design doc, a review session with a security engineer when the design is draft, and a final threat-model sign-off before any service handling user data ships to production.

The product roadmap is organized into three horizons: horizon one is scoped quarterly and tracked in Jira, horizon two is annual themes without firm dates reviewed at the start of each quarter, and horizon three is aspirational directions revisited yearly at an offsite.

The incident-response process is organized around three parallel roles that are always filled during a Sev-1: an incident commander who owns decisions and is the only person who can declare the incident over, a communications lead who owns the status page and internal updates on a fixed cadence, and a technical investigator who runs debugging while the commander shields them from questions.

The RFC process moves through four states: draft authored by the proposer, open review with a two-week comment window and a required summary of objections, decision with either acceptance or deferral recorded by a designated approver, and implementation tracking where the RFC is linked from every pull request that lands the change and the RFC is marked final only after a post-implementation review.

Our release train leaves every Tuesday: code freezes Monday at noon, a release candidate is cut and deployed to staging, on-call engineers across teams validate their surfaces against a shared checklist, a go/no-go meeting at 9am Tuesday approves the rollout, and a progressive deploy runs through canary, ten percent, fifty percent, and full over the next six hours.

The performance-review cycle is organized as a six-month loop: self-reflection written in the first week, peer feedback gathered through a structured form from four to six colleagues in the second, manager assessment drawing on both sources in the third week, a calibration meeting across managers in the fourth, and a two-week delivery window where each manager shares the outcome with their reports.

The hiring committee is structured as a two-tier review: an initial packet review by a three-person committee that either advances, rejects, or requests additional interviews, and a senior committee that makes the final call on advanced packets, with each committee rotating membership every quarter and an explicit recusal process for anyone who has worked with the candidate in the past.

The post-mortem workflow begins with a 24-hour draft written by the commander, a 48-hour technical review circulated to all involved engineers with line-comment resolution tracked in the document, a 72-hour blameless review meeting attended by the broader team with specific action items assigned to named owners, and a 30-day follow-up where the facilitator confirms the action items have landed or been explicitly deprioritized.

The product-spec process layers three documents: a one-pager with the problem framing that gets circulated to leadership for directional sign-off, a full PRD with detailed requirements and open questions reviewed by engineering and design, and a technical design doc authored by the lead engineer that references the PRD and goes through a separate engineering review before any implementation begins.

The security-incident escalation ladder has five rungs: on-call triage acknowledges and classifies the event, a security engineer opens a formal incident if classification is amber or higher, the security manager is paged for red classifications, the CISO is looped in for any incident with confirmed data exfiltration, and the general counsel is engaged within one hour whenever regulated data is involved.

Our change-management workflow for the production database has three gates: an automated diff posted by the migration bot to a shared review channel, a synchronous pairing session with a DBA to walk through the plan and expected lock impact, and a scheduled maintenance-window deployment that requires a rollback script committed alongside the migration and verified against a restored backup.

The documentation system is layered as five tiers: inline code comments for local invariants, ADRs capturing architectural decisions in-repo, a Backstage TechDocs site generated from markdown in each repo, a shared Notion workspace for cross-team playbooks, and a quarterly curation pass that prunes stale content and promotes high-traffic pages into a more authoritative location.
My monthly budget is split into three buckets: fifty percent for essentials, thirty percent for discretionary spending, and twenty percent for savings.
Our meal plan rotates over two weeks with a fixed theme per day: pasta Mondays, stir-fry Tuesdays, and so on.

The smart home is organized into three zones: the living area has lights and a thermostat, the bedrooms are on motion-activated lighting only, and the garage is on a separate security-focused automation group.

Our household chores are divided by day: laundry and sheet-changing on Sunday, a mid-week tidy and groceries on Wednesday, a full clean on Saturday morning, and a rolling bathroom-deep-clean that rotates between the three bathrooms on Fridays.

My investment portfolio is structured as sixty percent global equity index funds, twenty-five percent domestic bonds, ten percent real estate through a REIT index, and five percent set aside as a cash buffer for opportunistic rebalancing.

The family calendar has three overlapping layers: a shared household layer with chores and meal plans, a per-person work layer with do-not-disturb windows, and a kids layer with school and activity schedules that both parents can edit.

Our home network is split into a trusted VLAN for laptops and phones, an IoT VLAN with outbound internet only, a guest VLAN with bandwidth limits, and a dedicated VLAN for the media server that can reach the NAS but nothing else.

The personal-finance workflow has transactions synced from the bank into YNAB, a weekly reconciliation every Sunday evening, a monthly rollup into a Google Sheet with category trends, and a quarterly review where budgets are adjusted based on the last three months of actuals.

My reading system is organized in three stages: a capture inbox in Readwise Reader with anything interesting I find, a weekly triage where items are either archived or moved into a deep-read list, and a monthly review where notes from the deep-read items are distilled into Obsidian.

The weekly meal plan rotates on a two-week cycle of themes, with proteins purchased in bulk on Sundays, produce picked up midweek on Thursday, and a leftover-night slot on Friday that absorbs whatever didn't get eaten earlier.

Our home storage is structured around three zones: a daily-access layer in the main closets, a seasonal layer in underbed bins rotated twice a year, and an archival layer in the basement with labeled boxes indexed in a spreadsheet.

The household budget is layered into a baseline tier covering rent, utilities, groceries, and insurance on autopay from the main checking account; a discretionary tier funded through a weekly automated transfer into a separate debit card that acts as a hard cap; and a savings tier split across three sub-accounts for emergencies, annual expenses, and long-term goals, each with its own automated monthly contribution.

My home automation is organized as three coordinating layers: a device layer of Zigbee and Matter devices talking to a local Home Assistant instance, an intent layer of Node-RED flows that compose raw device events into semantic actions like 'bedtime' or 'leaving home', and a presentation layer of a tablet dashboard and voice assistants that only invoke the intent layer so nothing upstream depends on specific devices.

The personal knowledge system layers daily notes for ephemeral capture, project notes grouped under active goals, evergreen notes written in my own words that distill patterns across projects, and a quarterly review process where daily-note highlights are either promoted into project notes, absorbed into evergreens, or archived into a dated cold-storage folder.

Our retirement plan is structured as four concurrent accounts: a tax-deferred 401(k) maxed through payroll, a Roth IRA filled early each year through a backdoor conversion, a taxable brokerage holding tax-efficient index funds, and an HSA invested after the cash deductible buffer is covered, with rebalancing decisions made across the whole portfolio annually to keep target allocations constant.

The weekly schedule is organized around three energy tiers: deep-work mornings blocked off with no meetings and phone on do-not-disturb, collaborative afternoons reserved for pairing and reviews, and admin Fridays for expense reports, inbox zero, and planning the following week, with Wednesdays kept meeting-free as a buffer for emergent priorities.

Our meal system is a two-tier prep architecture: a Sunday bulk-cook session produces four protein bases and three grain bases stored in labeled containers, and weeknight assembly combines those bases with fresh vegetables and sauces from a rotating shortlist, so that dinner composition is a fast decision over an inventory rather than a recipe lookup.

The family's digital-access structure layers a password manager vault shared between the adults, a separate vault for the kids' accounts with parental shared items, a second-factor device tier where every high-value account is tied to two physical security keys stored in different rooms, and an offline recovery envelope in a safe with handwritten recovery phrases and instructions for a trusted executor.

My personal backup architecture follows the three-two-one rule in layers: a local Time Machine snapshot on a desk-side SSD for quick recovery, a NAS with nightly Restic snapshots of all devices accessible across the home network, and an encrypted offsite copy pushed weekly to a cloud provider with a rotating two-year retention window, plus an annual cold restore drill to validate the whole chain.

Our household emergency plan is structured in three tiers: a go-bag by the front door with seventy-two hours of essentials, a shelter-in-place tier in the basement with a week of water and food, and a remote tier with a cloud-backed document inventory and a documented out-of-state contact.
